question.problem:
Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on the set $A=\{0,1,2,3,4\},$ defined by 

$$
\{(0,0),(1,1),(1,4),(2,2),(3,3),(4,1),(4,4)\}.
$$

 How many distinct equivalence classes does $∼$ partition $A$ into?
question.worked_solution:
The equivalence classes of $∼$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a\in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & =\{a\in A∣a∼0\} \\  & =\{0\}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}[1] & =\{a\in A∣a∼1\} \\  & =\{1,4\}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}[2] & =\{a\in A∣a∼2\} \\  & =\{2\}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}[3] & =\{a\in A∣a∼3\} \\  & =\{3\}\end{aligned}
$$

We  skip $[4]$ since we already know that $4\in [1]$

All of the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $4$ distinct equivalence classes:

$$
[0]=\{0\},\,[1]=\{1,4\},\,[2]=\{2\},\,[3]=\{3\}.
$$

Notice that the equivalence classes form a partition of $A,$ as expected.
